name: Architecture & Design
tagline: Shape useful places and experiences, from first models to a critical research studio.

nodes.title: Spaces for Playing, Resting, and Sharing
nodes.goal: Describe what a place is used for and arrange a pretend space around a simple need.
learning_outcomes: Connect a place with an activity.
Leave a clear route between parts of a model.
Explain one arrangement choice using someone’s needs.

lesson.overview: Designing a space starts with what people want to do there. A place for a noisy game may need open room, while a place to listen to a story may need a comfortable gathering spot. Paths connect places so people can reach them. A model made from blocks or drawings lets us try arrangements before changing a real room. There can be several good arrangements because people and activities differ; the designer’s job is to listen and explain choices.
lesson.worked_example: Two dolls want to read while one wants to roll a toy car. A child places the reading mat beside the book basket and leaves a separate clear path for the car. The dolls can reach both areas without climbing over the basket.
lesson.activity: Build a pretend room with large blocks and paper furniture. Give it a reading place and a play place, then move a toy person through the paths.
lesson.reflection: How could your room change when more friends arrive?

quiz.prompt: What is a useful first question when making a pretend room?
choices: What will people do here?
Which path should I block?
Where can I hide the toys?
quiz.answer: What will people do here?
quiz.explain: Knowing the activity helps you choose the arrangement.
quiz.say: What is a useful first question when making a pretend room?

quiz.prompt: A doll wants a quiet story. Which place fits that wish?
choices: The middle of the noisy racing game
A closed box with no opening
A calm reading corner
quiz.answer: A calm reading corner
quiz.explain: A calm area can support listening to a story.
quiz.say: A doll wants a quiet story. Which place fits that wish?

quiz.prompt: Why leave a path through the model room?
choices: To make the room impossible to use
So people can reach its places
So no one can move
quiz.answer: So people can reach its places
quiz.explain: Paths connect activities and let people travel between them.
quiz.say: Why leave a path through the model room?

quiz.prompt: Can two rooms for the same game look different?
choices: Yes
No, the furniture must stay in one place
No, a game fixes the room’s shape
quiz.answer: Yes
quiz.explain: Several arrangements can support the same activity.
quiz.say: Can two rooms for the same game look different?

quiz.prompt: Your friend cannot reach the book basket in the model. What could help?
choices: Add more blocks in the path
Move the books farther away
Move the blocks that block the way
quiz.answer: Move the blocks that block the way
quiz.explain: Changing the arrangement can make the basket easier to reach.
quiz.say: Your friend cannot reach the book basket in the model. What could help?

quiz.prompt: What is a room model?
choices: A finished drawing that stays fixed
A small representation to try ideas
A full-sized room made for people
quiz.answer: A small representation to try ideas
quiz.explain: Models help us explore ideas and can be changed as we learn.
quiz.say: What is a room model?

nodes.kid_text: Make a little room for toys. Where will they play? Where will they rest? Leave a path so they can reach each place. Tell someone why you put things there.

nodes.title: Shapes Make Shelters
nodes.goal: Recognize basic shelter parts and combine shapes in a model with an entrance.
learning_outcomes: Identify roof, support, and entrance in a simple model.
Use shapes to create a covered space.
Recognize that an opening must fit its intended user.

lesson.overview: A shelter makes a place with some protection from its surroundings. Walls, roofs, supports, and openings can have different shapes and materials. A roof covers a space, and an entrance connects inside and outside. Real shelters vary with climate, available materials, culture, and purpose, so they do not all look like the same drawing of a house. A simple model can show parts and spaces, but a toy shelter is not evidence that a full-sized building would be safe.
lesson.worked_example: A child places a folded card roof across two block walls. There is a covered space below and a gap at the front for a toy. When another block fills that gap, the toy cannot enter, showing why an opening is part of the design.
lesson.activity: With adult help, make a low shelter for a toy using large blocks and card. Point to the roof, supports, inside, outside, and entrance.
lesson.reflection: What changes if your toy is taller than the entrance?

quiz.prompt: Which part goes over the sheltered space?
choices: The roof
The floor beneath it
The path outside
quiz.answer: The roof
quiz.explain: The roof covers a space from above.
quiz.say: Which part goes over the sheltered space?

quiz.prompt: What does an entrance let a toy do?
choices: Turn into a tree
Hold the roof above the walls
Move between outside and inside
quiz.answer: Move between outside and inside
quiz.explain: An entrance is an opening for passing into or out of a space.
quiz.say: What does an entrance let a toy do?

quiz.prompt: A tall toy cannot fit through a low opening. What could you change?
choices: Add a block in the opening
Make the opening taller
Make it even lower
quiz.answer: Make the opening taller
quiz.explain: An opening needs enough space for its intended user.
quiz.say: A tall toy cannot fit through a low opening. What could you change?

quiz.prompt: Do all shelters have exactly the same shape?
choices: No
Yes, shelters must be cubes
Yes, a shelter has a fixed shape
quiz.answer: No
quiz.explain: Shelters take many forms for different purposes and places.
quiz.say: Do all shelters have exactly the same shape?

quiz.prompt: What holds up the card roof in a block model?
choices: The empty air above it
The toy’s name
The supports beneath it
quiz.answer: The supports beneath it
quiz.explain: Supports transfer the roof’s load toward the surface beneath the model.
quiz.say: What holds up the card roof in a block model?

quiz.prompt: Does a toy shelter prove a big building is safe?
choices: Yes, if it is colorful
No
Yes, the toy’s size proves it
quiz.answer: No
quiz.explain: Full-sized buildings face different loads, materials, connections, and safety requirements.
quiz.say: Does a toy shelter prove a big building is safe?

nodes.kid_text: Use shapes to make a shelter for a toy. Add a roof, something to hold it up, and an opening. Can the toy get inside?

nodes.title: Measure and Draw a Simple Plan
nodes.goal: Measure a small space and represent positions in a labeled view from above.
learning_outcomes: Use one consistent unit to compare lengths.
Represent a small layout from above.
Explain symbols and identify information missing from a plan.

lesson.overview: A plan is a view looking down on a space. It can show where walls, doors, furniture, and paths are positioned even when we cannot see every surface from above in real life. Measurement helps a drawing relate to a real space. Using the same unit makes lengths comparable, and a simple grid can stand for equal floor distances. A legend explains symbols. Plans are useful for trying furniture arrangements, but they need other views to show heights and cannot communicate every experience of a place.
lesson.worked_example: A toy room is six blocks wide and four blocks deep. On grid paper, one square represents one block. Its outline is six squares by four. A table two blocks wide takes two grid squares, so it should not be drawn as a tiny dot.
lesson.activity: Measure a tabletop model in equal blocks or centimetres with adult help. Draw a top view with a door symbol, two objects, a clear path, and a legend.
lesson.reflection: What can your plan show clearly, and what does it leave out?

quiz.prompt: A floor plan usually shows a space from which direction?
choices: From above
From deep underground
From behind a chair
quiz.answer: From above
quiz.explain: A plan represents the arrangement in a horizontal view from above.
quiz.say: A floor plan usually shows a space from which direction?

quiz.prompt: One grid square stands for one block. A table is three blocks wide. How wide is it on the grid?
choices: One square
Ten squares
Three squares
quiz.answer: Three squares
quiz.explain: The representation uses the same one-to-one block-to-square rule.
quiz.say: One grid square stands for one block. A table is three blocks wide. How wide is it on the grid?

quiz.prompt: Why use the same measuring unit for two lengths?
choices: To avoid measuring
So the numbers can be compared directly
To make the objects equal in length
quiz.answer: So the numbers can be compared directly
quiz.explain: Consistent units give the numbers the same meaning.
quiz.say: Why use the same measuring unit for two lengths?

quiz.prompt: What does a legend explain?
choices: What the drawing’s symbols mean
Who owns the building
The weather tomorrow
quiz.answer: What the drawing’s symbols mean
quiz.explain: A legend connects symbols to the things they represent.
quiz.say: What does a legend explain?

quiz.prompt: Which feature is difficult to judge from a simple top-view plan alone?
choices: Where the shelf sits on the floor
Whether a drawn path crosses the room
The height of a shelf
quiz.answer: The height of a shelf
quiz.explain: A top view mainly shows horizontal positions; height needs another view or note.
quiz.say: Which feature is difficult to judge from a simple top-view plan alone?

quiz.prompt: A drawn chair blocks the door path. What can you do before moving real furniture?
choices: Erase the door from reality
Try a different position on the plan
Ignore the path
quiz.answer: Try a different position on the plan
quiz.explain: A plan lets you explore changes cheaply before rearranging objects.
quiz.say: A drawn chair blocks the door path. What can you do before moving real furniture?

nodes.kid_text: Look down on your toy room and draw where things go. Use the same little unit to measure each side. Add a key so a friend understands your symbols.

nodes.title: Listen to Users and Make a Prototype
nodes.goal: Listen to a user’s stated need, build a simple prototype, and revise it from observed use.
learning_outcomes: Ask about a user’s task before choosing a design.
Observe use of a low-risk prototype.
Revise a specific feature in response to evidence.

lesson.overview: A design serves people, and people do not all want or use things in the same way. Listening means asking about a need without assuming the answer. A prototype is an early model that helps test an idea, such as a cardboard book stand or a paper sign. We can observe whether someone can use it for the intended task and invite them to explain difficulties. Their difficulty is information about the design, not a reason to blame the user. Changes should respond to that evidence.
lesson.worked_example: A child makes a book stand for a friend who wants both hands free while drawing. The first prototype hides the bottom line of the page. After watching the friend try it, the designer lowers the front edge and tests again.
lesson.activity: Ask a family member about a low-risk task such as finding a bookmark. Draw or build a paper prototype, let them try it, and change one feature based on their feedback.
lesson.reflection: What did the user do that you did not expect?

quiz.prompt: What should you ask before designing a book stand?
choices: How will you use the book?
Which idea of mine must you like?
Why should users like my first idea?
quiz.answer: How will you use the book?
quiz.explain: Understanding the task helps shape a useful design.
quiz.say: What should you ask before designing a book stand?

quiz.prompt: The stand hides a line of text. What does that observation suggest?
choices: The reader is using eyes incorrectly
The book’s words should be removed
The front edge may need changing
quiz.answer: The front edge may need changing
quiz.explain: The prototype obstructs the task, so its shape is worth revising.
quiz.say: The stand hides a line of text. What does that observation suggest?

quiz.prompt: Why let someone try a prototype?
choices: To avoid changing anything
They may find an unexpected difficulty
To force them to praise it
quiz.answer: They may find an unexpected difficulty
quiz.explain: Actual use can reveal problems that a designer’s imagination misses.
quiz.say: Why let someone try a prototype?

quiz.prompt: Which question invites useful feedback?
choices: What was hard to do?
You loved everything, right?
Will you say I am the best?
quiz.answer: What was hard to do?
quiz.explain: An open question makes it easier to describe a real difficulty.
quiz.say: Which question invites useful feedback?

quiz.prompt: Do two users always need the same design?
choices: Yes, we have the same hands and tasks
Yes, the same task means the same need
No
quiz.answer: No
quiz.explain: Different abilities, preferences, and activities can lead to different needs.
quiz.say: Do two users always need the same design?

quiz.prompt: What makes a revision useful?
choices: It adds decoration without testing
It responds to a need or test result
It changes something at random
quiz.answer: It responds to a need or test result
quiz.explain: A purposeful change connects evidence to improved performance or experience.
quiz.say: What makes a revision useful?

nodes.kid_text: Ask someone what they need. Make a quick model and watch them try it. If something is hard to use, change the design and try again together.

nodes.title: Scale, Plans, Sections, and Models
nodes.goal: Convert simple drawing scales and use complementary views to explain a three-dimensional space.
learning_outcomes: Convert between drawing and full-size lengths.
Distinguish plan, elevation, and section.
Check consistency across representations and state model limits.

lesson.overview: A scaled drawing preserves ratios between represented lengths and real lengths. At 1:50, one centimetre on paper represents fifty centimetres in the space. A plan shows horizontal arrangement, an elevation shows a vertical face, and a section shows what an imaginary cut passes through. Each representation hides some information, so designers combine them. A physical or digital model can clarify volume and relationships, but miniature materials and lighting may behave differently from their full-sized counterparts. Units, orientation, and clear labels make drawings usable by others.
lesson.worked_example: At scale 1:50, a four-metre wall is 400/50 = 8 centimetres long on paper. A plan locates a window along that wall; an elevation shows its height, and a section can show wall thickness and the relationship of floor to ceiling.
lesson.activity: Draw a fictional small room at 1:50 with stated units. Add one elevation and one section, checking that a door’s position and height agree across views.
lesson.reflection: What could someone misunderstand if you gave them only one view?

quiz.prompt: At 1:50, a 2 cm line represents what real length?
choices: 100 cm
25 cm
2.5 cm
quiz.answer: 100 cm
quiz.explain: Multiply the drawing length by 50: 2 × 50 = 100 cm.

quiz.prompt: A real wall is 3 m long. How long is it at 1:100?
choices: 30 cm
300 cm
3 cm
quiz.answer: 3 cm
quiz.explain: Three metres is 300 cm; dividing by 100 gives 3 cm on paper.

quiz.prompt: Which view best shows an imaginary cut through a room?
choices: A plan
A section
An elevation
quiz.answer: A section
quiz.explain: A section reveals relationships at a defined cut, including internal heights or thicknesses.

quiz.prompt: Which view shows a building face straight on?
choices: An elevation
A plan
A cut through the interior
quiz.answer: An elevation
quiz.explain: An elevation represents a vertical face without cutting through the building.

quiz.prompt: Why include a scale bar when a drawing may be resized?
choices: The written ratio updates when printed
The bar corrects original dimension errors
The scale bar resizes with the drawing
quiz.answer: The scale bar resizes with the drawing
quiz.explain: A graphical reference changes with the drawing, unlike a written ratio that may become invalid after resizing.

quiz.prompt: A door is left of a window in the plan but right in the same oriented elevation. What needs checking?
choices: Check label order
Check orientation and consistency across views
Check which side has the longer room name
quiz.answer: Check orientation and consistency across views
quiz.explain: Views must describe one coherent arrangement, taking viewpoint and orientation into account.

quiz.prompt: At the same scale, a 4 m wall should be how long compared with a 2 m wall?
choices: Twice as long
The same length
Four times as long
quiz.answer: Twice as long
quiz.explain: A consistent scale preserves length ratios.

quiz.prompt: Which information must accompany the number 4 on a dimension?
choices: A color
A revision date and project title
A unit or established unit convention
quiz.answer: A unit or established unit convention
quiz.explain: Without units or an established convention, the represented length is ambiguous.

quiz.prompt: Does a cardboard model prove full-size structural performance?
choices: Yes; the shape matches
No; scale and material behavior differ
Yes; all proportional models reproduce structural capacity
quiz.answer: No; scale and material behavior differ
quiz.explain: Geometric similarity alone does not reproduce loads, stiffness, connections, and other physical behavior.

quiz.prompt: Why combine a model with drawings?
choices: Each reveals complementary spatial information
Models prove safety
Drawings determine comfort
quiz.answer: Each reveals complementary spatial information
quiz.explain: Complementary views help communicate arrangement, volume, dimensions, and details.

quiz.prompt: At 1:50, a model-room wall is 7 cm on paper. Convert it to metres and explain why an elevation is still needed to understand a window.
quiz.answer: The real wall is 350 cm, or 3.5 metres. A plan locates the window horizontally, but an elevation shows its vertical position and height. The views should agree on the same window and orientation.
quiz.explain: The real wall is 350 cm, or 3.5 metres. A plan locates the window horizontally, but an elevation shows its vertical position and height. The views should agree on the same window and orientation.

nodes.title: Inclusive Design and Accessible Experiences
nodes.goal: Identify barriers in an everyday design and propose multiple ways to access the same task.
learning_outcomes: Explain a barrier as a person-design interaction.
Provide more than one cue for important information.
Evaluate a prototype with diverse needs and acknowledge representation limits.

lesson.overview: Inclusive design considers differences in bodies, senses, language, attention, experience, and circumstances. A barrier may arise from the interaction between a person and a design rather than from the person alone. A sign that uses color without words can be unclear to some viewers, while a heavy door can exclude people carrying bags as well as people with limited strength. Designers seek multiple ways to perceive information and perform tasks, test with diverse users, and remain open to needs that were not initially represented. Accessibility is not established by a single simulation or by assuming one user represents everyone.
lesson.worked_example: A recycling station has three bins distinguished only by red, green, and blue. Adding clear words, pictures, and distinct positions gives users more ways to identify a bin. Testing still matters because pictures can also be confusing or culturally unfamiliar.
lesson.activity: Audit a fictional library sign and entrance using a task-based checklist. Identify three barriers and prototype one change using words, symbols, contrast, or an alternate route. Ask for feedback without pretending to speak for an entire group.
lesson.reflection: Who was missing from your test, and how could that affect your confidence?

quiz.prompt: A sign communicates only through red and green. What improvement adds another route to understanding?
choices: Add clear words or recognizable symbols
Increase the number of red and green shades
Reduce the text and expand the colored areas
quiz.answer: Add clear words or recognizable symbols
quiz.explain: Redundant cues reduce reliance on a single visual distinction.

quiz.prompt: Why is a heavy door an inclusive-design issue?
choices: Door weight determines everyone’s access equally
Heavy doors primarily create a labeling problem
Users differ in strength and circumstances
quiz.answer: Users differ in strength and circumstances
quiz.explain: Ability and circumstances vary, including injury, carrying objects, or mobility differences.

quiz.prompt: What is a barrier in design?
choices: A design feature with an unfamiliar visual style
A condition that makes a task harder to access
A numerical rating of a user’s general ability
quiz.answer: A condition that makes a task harder to access
quiz.explain: Barriers emerge when the design does not support the user’s abilities or circumstances.

quiz.prompt: One user succeeds with a prototype. What does this show?
choices: Success for that user, task, and test setting
Success for each user in the target population
Success under changed tasks and surroundings
quiz.answer: Success for that user, task, and test setting
quiz.explain: A successful test is useful evidence but has a limited scope.

quiz.prompt: Why test symbols instead of assuming they are obvious?
choices: Pictograms carry a fixed culture-free meaning
Symbols are understood through their color alone
Interpretations can vary across experience
quiz.answer: Interpretations can vary across experience
quiz.explain: Experience and culture influence how symbols are understood.

quiz.prompt: Which question is most useful in a task-based audit?
choices: Does the entrance look similar to nearby buildings?
Can a visitor find and use the entrance?
Does the entrance use the designer’s favorite shape?
quiz.answer: Can a visitor find and use the entrance?
quiz.explain: An audit should focus on whether people can achieve the intended task.

quiz.prompt: Why offer an alternative to an audio-only instruction?
choices: Hearing ability and listening conditions vary
Audio instructions are less informative by definition
Printed words provide equal access in each language
quiz.answer: Hearing ability and listening conditions vary
quiz.explain: Text or visual instructions can support different sensory abilities and contexts.

quiz.prompt: Does briefly simulating a disability make a designer an expert on that lived experience?
choices: Yes; a brief simulation provides equivalent expertise
Yes; simulation removes the need for user involvement
No; simulation does not reproduce lived experience
quiz.answer: No; simulation does not reproduce lived experience
quiz.explain: A simulation cannot reproduce the range, adaptation, and context of lived experience.

quiz.prompt: Which feedback response supports inclusive design?
choices: Exclude the difficult task from further evaluation
Investigate the difficulty and revise the design
Train the user to accept the current arrangement
quiz.answer: Investigate the difficulty and revise the design
quiz.explain: Difficulties reveal possible barriers and should inform learning.

quiz.prompt: Why record who participated in testing?
choices: To show the sample’s coverage and its gaps
To establish representation from participant count
To determine a ranking of users’ design preferences
quiz.answer: To show the sample’s coverage and its gaps
quiz.explain: Participant context helps readers judge whose needs were and were not examined.

quiz.prompt: A route map uses colors without labels, and one test participant succeeds. Explain two improvements to the design process.
quiz.answer: Add words or symbols so color is not the sole cue. Test relevant tasks with diverse users and circumstances, recording barriers and missing perspectives. One participant’s success gives limited evidence and does not establish accessibility for everyone.
quiz.explain: Add words or symbols so color is not the sole cue. Test relevant tasks with diverse users and circumstances, recording barriers and missing perspectives. One participant’s success gives limited evidence and does not establish accessibility for everyone.

visual_spec.title: More than one cue supports access

items.heading: Words and shapes

items.detail: Additional ways to identify the route.

items.heading: User testing

items.detail: Find barriers the design team missed.

visual_spec.takeaway: Redundant cues help, and real use still needs testing.

nodes.title: Buildings, Climate, and Passive Strategies
nodes.goal: Relate sun, airflow, material properties, and site conditions to design choices while evaluating seasonal tradeoffs.
learning_outcomes: Distinguish insulation, thermal mass, shading, and ventilation.
Connect passive strategies to site and seasonal conditions.
State limits of simplified comfort and energy claims.

lesson.overview: Buildings exchange heat, air, moisture, and light with their surroundings. Orientation and shading affect solar gains, insulation slows heat transfer through the envelope, and ventilation exchanges indoor and outdoor air. Thermal mass stores heat and releases it over time; it is not interchangeable with insulation. A strategy that helps in one climate or season can create problems in another, and real comfort also depends on occupancy, clothing, activity, air movement, and expectations. Early diagrams guide questions, but performance claims require suitable calculations, measurements, and local requirements.
lesson.worked_example: A west-facing window receives low afternoon sun. A simple horizontal overhang may shade it less effectively than it shades a high midday sun angle. The designer compares shading geometry across times and seasons rather than assuming one sketch proves year-round comfort.
lesson.activity: Study a fictional site in two seasons. Draw sun paths conceptually, possible airflow routes, shaded areas, and envelope layers. Compare two design strategies using explicit assumptions and identify a potential unintended effect.
lesson.reflection: When might blocking solar gain help in one season and be undesirable in another?

quiz.prompt: What is the main function of insulation in a building envelope?
choices: Reduce heat transfer through the envelope
Store heat for release later in the day
Increase air exchange through the enclosure
quiz.answer: Reduce heat transfer through the envelope
quiz.explain: Insulation provides thermal resistance; its effect depends on installation and the whole assembly.

quiz.prompt: What distinguishes thermal mass from insulation?
choices: Mass resists flow; insulation generates heat
Mass blocks airflow; insulation stores moisture
Mass stores heat; insulation resists flow
quiz.answer: Mass stores heat; insulation resists flow
quiz.explain: Heat capacity and thermal resistance describe different physical behaviors.

quiz.prompt: Why may a horizontal overhang poorly block low-angle sun?
choices: Overhang shade is independent of solar geometry
Low rays may pass beneath the overhang
Low-angle rays have negligible thermal energy
quiz.answer: Low rays may pass beneath the overhang
quiz.explain: Shading effectiveness depends on geometry and solar angle.

quiz.prompt: Which factor can change a passive design’s performance across the year?
choices: Seasonal sun angles and outdoor conditions
The project title and exterior color palette
The number of simulation images in the report
quiz.answer: Seasonal sun angles and outdoor conditions
quiz.explain: A strategy responds to environmental conditions, which vary over time.

quiz.prompt: Does opening windows always improve thermal comfort?
choices: Yes; opening windows implies cooler indoor air
Yes; air exchange determines comfort independently
No; outdoor conditions and airflow matter
quiz.answer: No; outdoor conditions and airflow matter
quiz.explain: Ventilation can help or hinder depending on temperature, air quality, noise, safety, and airflow.

quiz.prompt: What does orientation influence?
choices: Heat capacity of the building’s structural mass
Solar exposure of surfaces over time
Thermal conductivity of the wall material
quiz.answer: Solar exposure of surfaces over time
quiz.explain: Orientation changes the exposure of walls and openings to the sun and local conditions.

quiz.prompt: A sketch shows an airflow arrow. What does it establish?
choices: An intended path requiring verification
A measured ventilation-rate prediction
A validated indoor-air-quality outcome
quiz.answer: An intended path requiring verification
quiz.explain: An arrow represents a hypothesis; actual flow depends on pressure differences, openings, and obstructions.

quiz.prompt: Why include occupants in a building-performance model?
choices: Occupants determine material thermal conductivity
Schedules replace the need for weather information
Activities and actions influence conditions
quiz.answer: Activities and actions influence conditions
quiz.explain: Internal gains, window use, and comfort needs depend on occupancy.

quiz.prompt: A strategy reduces summer gains but increases winter heating demand. What is this?
choices: A numerical rounding inconsistency
A seasonal performance tradeoff
A violation of energy conservation
quiz.answer: A seasonal performance tradeoff
quiz.explain: Design often balances effects across periods and objectives.

quiz.prompt: What supports a defensible performance claim beyond an early diagram?
choices: Suitable analysis or measurements with assumptions
A bright rendering with consistent camera exposure
A precedent image from a visually similar building
quiz.answer: Suitable analysis or measurements with assumptions
quiz.explain: Evidence and assumptions are needed to assess the claimed thermal or energy behavior.

quiz.prompt: A designer copies a large unshaded west window from a cool-climate project into a hot site. Explain why the precedent is insufficient and what to study.
quiz.answer: The new climate and orientation change solar gains and comfort demands. Study low-angle afternoon sun, shading geometry, glazing and envelope properties, and seasonal tradeoffs using suitable analysis. A precedent or rendering does not validate performance in the new context.
quiz.explain: The new climate and orientation change solar gains and comfort demands. Study low-angle afternoon sun, shading geometry, glazing and envelope properties, and seasonal tradeoffs using suitable analysis. A precedent or rendering does not validate performance in the new context.

nodes.title: Visual Hierarchy, Information, and Wayfinding
nodes.goal: Design a coherent information system using hierarchy, contrast, spatial cues, and user testing.
learning_outcomes: Use visual hierarchy to communicate priority.
Place wayfinding information at appropriate decision points.
Evaluate task success separately from aesthetic preference.

lesson.overview: Information design helps people find, understand, and act on information. Hierarchy makes the most important content noticeable through size, position, spacing, and other cues. Wayfinding combines signs with spatial organization, landmarks, visibility, and consistent naming. A beautiful sign may still fail if placed after a decision point or if it uses unfamiliar terminology. Designers distinguish recognition from recall, avoid making color the only carrier of meaning, and evaluate real tasks such as locating a room rather than measuring preference alone.
lesson.worked_example: A library sign lists every room in equally small type after a corridor junction. A revised design places a short directional sign before the junction, uses the same room names as the map, and reserves larger type for destinations. A test asks visitors to find a room without coaching.
lesson.activity: Create a three-sign system for a fictional library: entry overview, junction direction, and room confirmation. Test a paper route with a peer, record wrong turns and questions, and revise the point causing confusion.
lesson.reflection: Could users like a design while still being unable to complete its task?

quiz.prompt: Where is a directional sign usually most useful?
choices: Before or at the decision point
After the visitor has passed the turn
At the center of the longest corridor
quiz.answer: Before or at the decision point
quiz.explain: Information should arrive in time to guide the decision.

quiz.prompt: What does visual hierarchy communicate?
choices: Estimated material and printing costs
The chronological order of design revisions
Content priority and reading sequence
quiz.answer: Content priority and reading sequence
quiz.explain: Size, spacing, position, and contrast guide attention and sequence.

quiz.prompt: A map says “Study Hall” but door signs say “Reading Zone.” What issue arises?
choices: Naming differences establish spatial hierarchy
Inconsistent names can disrupt navigation
Different names reduce reliance on memory
quiz.answer: Inconsistent names can disrupt navigation
quiz.explain: Consistent destination names help connect representations and real places.

quiz.prompt: Why measure wrong turns in a wayfinding test?
choices: They reveal navigation task difficulties
They measure preference for sign aesthetics
They determine visitors’ prior map-reading skill
quiz.answer: They reveal navigation task difficulties
quiz.explain: Navigation errors can identify unclear cues or decision points.

quiz.prompt: Which design supports recognition rather than recall?
choices: A memorized list of room numbers
A recalled sequence of earlier turns
A visible labeled destination list
quiz.answer: A visible labeled destination list
quiz.explain: Visible cues allow users to identify options without remembering them unaided.

quiz.prompt: Can a high preference rating alone prove successful wayfinding?
choices: Yes; visual quality establishes route accuracy
No; preference and task success differ
Yes; liking predicts unaided navigation
quiz.answer: No; preference and task success differ
quiz.explain: Aesthetic preference and task performance are distinct outcomes.

quiz.prompt: Why use whitespace between information groups?
choices: To make information groups easier to perceive
To maximize the quantity of text on each sign
To replace the need for destination naming
quiz.answer: To make information groups easier to perceive
quiz.explain: Spacing helps users perceive related items and separate different groups.

quiz.prompt: A color-coded route also has a shape and name. What does this add?
choices: A guarantee that users share symbol meanings
A substitute for observing route completion
Several consistent identification cues
quiz.answer: Several consistent identification cues
quiz.explain: Multiple consistent cues reduce dependence on color discrimination alone.

quiz.prompt: Why avoid coaching participants during a navigation test?
choices: Coaching makes the route physically inaccessible
Coaching can supply missing design information
Coaching changes the scale of printed symbols
quiz.answer: Coaching can supply missing design information
quiz.explain: Prompts can supply missing information and overstate unaided usability.

quiz.prompt: Which is part of wayfinding beyond signs?
choices: Spatial layout and recognizable landmarks
Printing dimensions and supplier invoices
Font licensing and sign-installation budgets
quiz.answer: Spatial layout and recognizable landmarks
quiz.explain: People use the organization of space and environmental cues as well as signs.

quiz.prompt: Visitors repeatedly miss a library turn even though they like the sign’s appearance. Explain how you would revise and evaluate the information system.
quiz.answer: Check whether the sign appears before the decision point and whether naming is consistent across signs and maps. Improve hierarchy and placement, then measure task success and wrong turns without coaching. Preference alone does not establish effective wayfinding.
quiz.explain: Check whether the sign appears before the decision point and whether naming is consistent across signs and maps. Improve hierarchy and placement, then measure task success and wrong turns without coaching. Preference alone does not establish effective wayfinding.

nodes.title: Spatial Systems and Building Performance
nodes.goal: Integrate spatial design with envelope, daylight, and circulation models while tracking assumptions and competing objectives.
learning_outcomes: Link spatial decisions to multiple performance systems.
Separate evidence-based inputs from uncertain assumptions.
Interpret spatial and temporal distributions alongside aggregate metrics.

lesson.overview: Building performance emerges from interacting systems rather than isolated components. Window area affects daylight, views, solar gains, and heat transfer; circulation affects access, travel, and usable floor area. A simulation encodes weather, geometry, materials, controls, and occupancy assumptions, while simplified models omit details to make analysis tractable. Good practice distinguishes inputs known from evidence, design choices, and uncertain assumptions. Comparing alternatives requires common boundaries and useful metrics, including distribution through space and time rather than an annual average alone. Technical performance must also be integrated with use, comfort, maintenance, and local professional requirements.
lesson.worked_example: Two layouts have the same average modeled daylight metric. In one, most desks receive moderate daylight; in the other, some receive very high exposure and others very little. The average hides a spatial distribution that could affect glare and equitable access to desirable workspaces.
lesson.activity: Compare two fictional room layouts using consistent weather and occupancy assumptions. Map daylight distribution, envelope area, and circulation distance. Run one sensitivity analysis, explain an unresolved tradeoff, and identify which result requires professional or empirical validation.
lesson.reflection: Which metric improves when you change the layout, and who experiences the improvement or loss?

quiz.prompt: Increasing window area can affect which combination?
choices: Daylight, views, heat transfer, and solar gains
Daylight, views, sound absorption, and soil permeability
Daylight, views, foundation depth, and material density
quiz.answer: Daylight, views, heat transfer, and solar gains
quiz.explain: A single design choice can influence several physical and experiential systems.

quiz.prompt: Why use common occupancy assumptions when comparing alternatives?
choices: To establish that future users have identical behavior
To remove uncertainty from predicted annual results
To isolate modeled design differences more clearly
quiz.answer: To isolate modeled design differences more clearly
quiz.explain: A consistent comparison isolates the modeled design difference while assumptions remain explicit.

quiz.prompt: Two layouts share the same mean daylight value. What may still differ?
choices: The total number of modeled daylight observations
Spatial distribution and extreme conditions
The mathematical definition of the arithmetic mean
quiz.answer: Spatial distribution and extreme conditions
quiz.explain: A mean can hide uneven conditions, glare risks, or poorly lit areas.

quiz.prompt: Which input is often uncertain in early design?
choices: Future schedules and occupant behavior
The specified definition of the length unit
The conservation principle in the energy balance
quiz.answer: Future schedules and occupant behavior
quiz.explain: Future use is variable and uncertain, so scenario or sensitivity analysis is useful.

quiz.prompt: What does sensitivity analysis contribute?
choices: Physical validity established independently of data
The ethically correct priority between design goals
Dependence on inputs and design assumptions
quiz.answer: Dependence on inputs and design assumptions
quiz.explain: Sensitivity exposes influential assumptions and the robustness of comparisons.

quiz.prompt: Why distinguish model calibration from independent validation?
choices: Validation is another name for choosing fitted parameters
Fitting and independent testing answer different questions
Calibration provides stronger transfer evidence by definition
quiz.answer: Fitting and independent testing answer different questions
quiz.explain: Agreement with fitted data does not establish performance on independent cases.

quiz.prompt: A route is shortest but excludes some users. What is missing from its evaluation?
choices: User requirements and accessible routes
The precision of the map’s printing process
The order of rooms in the project description
quiz.answer: User requirements and accessible routes
quiz.explain: Travel distance alone is insufficient if the route is not usable by intended users.

quiz.prompt: Why assess results over time rather than only annually?
choices: Annual energy totals have no mathematical meaning
Hourly conditions are interchangeable in operation
Peaks and occupied-period conditions may be hidden
quiz.answer: Peaks and occupied-period conditions may be hidden
quiz.explain: Temporal distribution matters for comfort, load peaks, and practical operation.

quiz.prompt: A photorealistic rendering looks bright. What can it establish about daylight performance?
choices: A demonstrated absence of glare under future occupancy
Visual intent without a validated performance analysis
A measured annual daylight distribution in the building
quiz.answer: Visual intent without a validated performance analysis
quiz.explain: Rendering brightness can reflect artistic settings and is not automatically physical evidence.

quiz.prompt: Why document maintenance assumptions?
choices: Upkeep can affect realized system performance
Maintenance determines the definition of energy efficiency
Documenting assumptions ensures identical future operation
quiz.answer: Upkeep can affect realized system performance
quiz.explain: Systems must remain operable for modeled performance to persist.

quiz.prompt: Two layouts have equal annual mean daylight scores, but one has very bright and very dim work areas. Explain the next analysis and the limitation of the mean.
quiz.answer: Map the spatial distribution and occupied-period conditions, including glare and low-light locations. The mean hides unequal exposure and temporal extremes. Compare alternatives with consistent assumptions and assess uncertainty before inferring comparable performance.
quiz.explain: Map the spatial distribution and occupied-period conditions, including glare and low-light locations. The mean hides unequal exposure and temporal extremes. Compare alternatives with consistent assumptions and assess uncertainty before inferring comparable performance.

nodes.title: Design Research and Post-Occupancy Evaluation
nodes.goal: Investigate how a designed environment performs in use using mixed evidence, ethical sampling, and transparent interpretation.
learning_outcomes: Choose complementary methods for specific design questions.
Identify response bias, timing, and observer effects.
Translate evidence into justified recommendations with privacy safeguards.

lesson.overview: Post-occupancy evaluation studies a place after people begin using it. Walkthroughs, interviews, surveys, behavior observations, and physical measurements reveal different aspects of experience. A questionnaire can describe reported comfort but should not be treated as a direct measurement of temperature or as proof of a causal design effect. Recruitment, response bias, timing, observer influence, and privacy affect the evidence. A useful evaluation connects observations to design decisions, includes users who are easy to miss, and distinguishes quick fixes from questions requiring deeper investigation.
lesson.worked_example: A new study room receives high satisfaction scores from daytime respondents, but evening users are scarcely represented. A follow-up recruits across time periods and pairs reports with lighting and occupancy observations. The revised evidence may explain an issue hidden by the first sample.
lesson.activity: Design a mock evaluation of a library using fictional or volunteered non-sensitive feedback. Define research questions, sampling times, observation measures, consent, privacy, and analysis. Triangulate two evidence types and write a recommendation proportional to the findings.
lesson.reflection: Whose experience is missing, and what would change your recommendation?

quiz.prompt: What does a comfort survey directly measure?
choices: Reported experience of the participants
Instrument-measured air temperature
An identified causal design effect
quiz.answer: Reported experience of the participants
quiz.explain: Self-reports are valuable evidence about experience but differ from physical measurements and causal estimates.

quiz.prompt: Only daytime users answer a survey. What limitation matters?
choices: The room has no relevant evening population
Daytime preference establishes evening requirements
Evening experiences may be underrepresented
quiz.answer: Evening experiences may be underrepresented
quiz.explain: Sampling coverage limits whose experience the findings describe.

quiz.prompt: Why combine interviews with physical measurements?
choices: Combined methods remove the need for sampling decisions
They answer complementary evidence questions
Each method independently confirms the other’s accuracy
quiz.answer: They answer complementary evidence questions
quiz.explain: Triangulation can reveal agreements and discrepancies among different kinds of evidence.

quiz.prompt: Observers stand beside a doorway and people change routes. What is a concern?
choices: The observer may influence the route choice
The route has become a randomized treatment
Observed movement is unaffected by measurement
quiz.answer: The observer may influence the route choice
quiz.explain: The act of observation can alter the behavior being studied.

quiz.prompt: What is a reasonable privacy practice for a small-space evaluation?
choices: Record conversations without explaining their use
Publish small-group quotations with inferred identities
Limit collection and avoid identifiable reporting
quiz.answer: Limit collection and avoid identifiable reporting
quiz.explain: Purpose-limited collection and careful reporting reduce unnecessary intrusion.

quiz.prompt: Which question suits a walkthrough?
choices: The exact causal effect of a selected wall color
Where visible obstructions interrupt a route
How occupants will feel after a decade of use
quiz.answer: Where visible obstructions interrupt a route
quiz.explain: A walkthrough can systematically inspect observable spatial conditions.

quiz.prompt: Why record observation times?
choices: Conditions and use may vary across time
Timestamps identify the causal mechanism
A date label guarantees a representative sample
quiz.answer: Conditions and use may vary across time
quiz.explain: Timing affects occupancy, light, noise, and who is represented.

quiz.prompt: A design feature correlates with satisfaction. What should the report avoid?
choices: Description of the observed association and uncertainty
Discussion of plausible alternative explanations
Causal attribution without an appropriate design
quiz.answer: Causal attribution without an appropriate design
quiz.explain: Other features or user differences can explain an observed association.

quiz.prompt: What makes a recommendation proportionate?
choices: The claim prioritizes agreement over contradictory evidence
The claim’s scope and certainty match the evidence
The claim adopts the strongest possible wording
quiz.answer: The claim’s scope and certainty match the evidence
quiz.explain: A recommendation should reflect both what was learned and what remains uncertain.

quiz.prompt: Why invite feedback from people who stopped using the space?
choices: They may reveal barriers missed by current users
Their experience is less relevant by definition
Their absence demonstrates satisfaction with the space
quiz.answer: They may reveal barriers missed by current users
quiz.explain: Nonuse and withdrawal can reveal exclusion or problems hidden among continuing users.

quiz.prompt: A library evaluation surveys daytime visitors and recommends removing evening lighting. Critique the sampling and propose a better evidence plan.
quiz.answer: The sample misses evening users and cannot justify that recommendation. Recruit across relevant times, combine reported experience with lighting measurements and observations, and protect privacy. Report uncertainty and align the recommendation with the population and conditions actually studied.
quiz.explain: The sample misses evening users and cannot justify that recommendation. Recruit across relevant times, combine reported experience with lighting measurements and observations, and protect privacy. Report uncertainty and align the recommendation with the population and conditions actually studied.

nodes.title: Performance-Based Design Research
nodes.goal: Develop a reproducible design experiment that separates exploration, optimization, validation, and critical interpretation.
learning_outcomes: Separate exploratory search, optimization, and confirmatory research.
Design reproducible parametric studies with validation and uncertainty.
Critique performance metrics in relation to user and spatial values.

lesson.overview: Performance-based design research uses explicit hypotheses and metrics to investigate how design choices influence outcomes. A parametric model can generate many alternatives, but more alternatives do not compensate for a weak model or narrow objective. Exploration identifies patterns; confirmatory testing assesses prespecified claims; optimization searches a defined problem; validation examines whether the model is credible for its intended use. Graduate work documents geometry, parameters, software, boundary conditions, and uncertainty, then interprets quantitative results alongside spatial quality and user needs. A research contribution should be distinguishable from simply producing an appealing final scheme.
lesson.worked_example: A parametric study varies window ratio and shading depth across a grid of designs. The researcher selects a promising region, reserves additional cases for validation, and tests sensitivity to occupancy and weather. A design with a slightly worse average energy score may be preferred if it reduces glare and performs more consistently across assumptions.
lesson.activity: Create a dissertation-style protocol for a simulated design question. Include a hypothesis, parameter domain, sampling plan, competing metrics, uncertainty analysis, validation strategy, reproducible files, and a critical discussion of what the metrics leave out. Compare at least two non-dominated alternatives.
lesson.reflection: Which part of your conclusion is a measured finding, which is model-dependent, and which is a value judgment?

quiz.prompt: What distinguishes a research contribution from a polished design alone?
choices: A justified question, method, evidence, and insight
An attractive final object
A portfolio of polished designs
quiz.answer: A justified question, method, evidence, and insight
quiz.explain: Research must make its reasoning and evidence assessable beyond the finished object.

quiz.prompt: A parametric model generates ten thousand options. What does this not guarantee?
choices: Many alternatives
Variation across the parameters selected for the search
Validity of assumptions and selected metrics
quiz.answer: Validity of assumptions and selected metrics
quiz.explain: Search volume cannot correct model-form errors or omitted values.

quiz.prompt: Why reserve cases for validation after model fitting?
choices: To choose validation criteria after seeing outcomes
To evaluate prediction beyond model fitting
To improve agreement on previously fitted cases
quiz.answer: To evaluate prediction beyond model fitting
quiz.explain: Independent evaluation helps detect overfitting and limits of generalization.

quiz.prompt: What belongs in a reproducible parametric-study record?
choices: Geometry rules, inputs, versions, and analysis code
Images and commentary
Every rendered view and its presentation order
quiz.answer: Geometry rules, inputs, versions, and analysis code
quiz.explain: Others need the generation and evaluation process, not just its final output.

quiz.prompt: One design uses less energy; another provides better glare control. What is the key issue?
choices: Arithmetic error
Proof that energy cannot inform any design decision
A tradeoff between competing objectives
quiz.answer: A tradeoff between competing objectives
quiz.explain: Competing objectives may favor different alternatives, requiring explicit priorities.

quiz.prompt: Why test occupancy scenarios?
choices: Behavior can be inferred from the final renderings
Use assumptions may change performance rankings
Occupancy schedules are fixed by the building geometry
quiz.answer: Use assumptions may change performance rankings
quiz.explain: Behavior and schedules change loads and conditions, so uncertainty can alter preferences.

quiz.prompt: Which practice separates confirmation from exploration?
choices: Prespecify the claim and evaluation criterion
Select a successful finding
Treat every explored result as a planned confirmation
quiz.answer: Prespecify the claim and evaluation criterion
quiz.explain: Prespecification clarifies the evidential status of a final test.

quiz.prompt: A model matches energy totals but misrepresents hourly peaks. What should be said?
choices: Every prediction is valid
The model is invalid for every possible application
Validation is incomplete for peak-related claims
quiz.answer: Validation is incomplete for peak-related claims
quiz.explain: Validity is tied to the quantity of interest and the intended use.

quiz.prompt: A metric omits privacy and autonomy. What is the implication?
choices: Ignore those values
Consider those values separately in the decision
Assume the metric captures every important social value
quiz.answer: Consider those values separately in the decision
quiz.explain: Quantification of selected outcomes does not exhaust the design’s human consequences.

quiz.prompt: What strengthens a model-dependent conclusion?
choices: Scope, assumptions, sensitivity, and conflicting evidence
The most favorable result and its visual presentation
A universal claim based on the best-performing variant
quiz.answer: Scope, assumptions, sensitivity, and conflicting evidence
quiz.explain: Transparent limitations allow others to judge how far the result can be trusted and transferred.

quiz.prompt: A parametric model selects the lowest-energy layout among 5,000 variants, all based on one occupancy schedule. Explain how to turn the result into a defensible research claim.
quiz.answer: Validate the model for the intended outcome, test sensitivity to occupancy and other uncertain assumptions, and compare additional metrics such as glare and accessibility. Document the reproducible search and distinguish the computed optimum from a general design recommendation.
quiz.explain: Validate the model for the intended outcome, test sensitivity to occupancy and other uncertain assumptions, and compare additional metrics such as glare and accessibility. Document the reproducible search and distinguish the computed optimum from a general design recommendation.

nodes.title: Participatory Design, Critique, and a Research Studio
nodes.goal: Conduct a critically reflective design inquiry with stakeholder participation, prototype evidence, and an accountable argument.
learning_outcomes: Design participation that addresses power and representation.
Use contrasting prototypes and reflective records to generate defensible insight.
Present a critical argument that includes dissent, limits, and evidence of influence.

lesson.overview: Participatory design gives people affected by a design meaningful influence over questions, alternatives, and evaluation. Participation is not established by inviting comments after all consequential decisions have been made. Power, compensation, language, access, and representation shape whose input is heard. Research through design uses making and testing to generate knowledge, while reflective documentation connects material decisions with hypotheses and learning. Graduate critique examines whose interests the brief serves, which perspectives are absent, how disagreement was handled, and whether the evidence supports claims beyond the local project.
lesson.worked_example: A library redesign workshop includes staff and frequent visitors but initially omits people who cannot access the building. The team revises recruitment, offers alternative participation formats, and records disagreements about quiet and social space. Two prototypes test different arrangements, and the final proposal explains both the chosen tradeoff and unresolved concerns.
lesson.activity: Prepare a research-studio portfolio for a fictional civic space. Include a stakeholder and power map, accessible participation plan, consent and attribution choices, two contrasting prototypes, task-based evidence, reflective notes, and a critical argument. Present a dissenting perspective fairly and revise one consequential decision in response.
lesson.reflection: Which decision did participants actually influence, and what evidence demonstrates that influence?

quiz.prompt: Which activity most clearly gives participants design influence?
choices: Participants shape criteria and consequential choices
Participants review the fixed scheme’s presentation
Participants provide attendance records for the report
quiz.answer: Participants shape criteria and consequential choices
quiz.explain: Meaningful participation affects the decisions, not merely the appearance of consultation.

quiz.prompt: Why analyze power among stakeholders?
choices: Workshop attendance gives participants equal authority
A stakeholder list determines each person’s priorities
Influence and exclusion differ among stakeholders
quiz.answer: Influence and exclusion differ among stakeholders
quiz.explain: Roles, resources, and institutions affect whose needs and interpretations prevail.

quiz.prompt: A workshop recruits only frequent users. What perspective may be missing?
choices: People with routine access to the workshop venue
People excluded by the existing space
People currently using the space frequently
quiz.answer: People excluded by the existing space
quiz.explain: Those who cannot or choose not to use the space may identify barriers that regular users overlook.

quiz.prompt: What makes a reflective design journal useful for research?
choices: It links decisions, evidence, and changing interpretations
It replaces outside evidence with the designer’s confidence
It records a finished account without abandoned alternatives
quiz.answer: It links decisions, evidence, and changing interpretations
quiz.explain: A traceable reflective record supports analysis of how making generated and revised knowledge.

quiz.prompt: Why test contrasting prototypes?
choices: To establish one arrangement as universally correct
To avoid specifying what the prototypes should test
To expose assumptions through alternative designs
quiz.answer: To expose assumptions through alternative designs
quiz.explain: Contrasting forms can reveal how different design choices shape tasks and experiences.

quiz.prompt: Participants disagree about noise and sociability. What is a defensible response?
choices: Remove conflicting comments before making a summary
Document disagreement and explain the tradeoff
Infer consensus from attendance at the same workshop
quiz.answer: Document disagreement and explain the tradeoff
quiz.explain: Participation need not produce unanimity; accountable design makes disagreement and choices visible.

quiz.prompt: Why offer multiple participation formats?
choices: Access, language, schedules, and format preferences differ
Public meetings provide equal participation opportunities
Additional formats eliminate the need to examine representation
quiz.answer: Access, language, schedules, and format preferences differ
quiz.explain: Alternative routes can widen participation while representation still requires scrutiny.

quiz.prompt: What should attribution of participant contributions consider?
choices: Automatic identification of attendees in the final report
The designer’s preferred credit order without consultation
Consent, preferences, and contribution type
quiz.answer: Consent, preferences, and contribution type
quiz.explain: Participants should have appropriate control over identification and recognition.

quiz.prompt: A successful local prototype supports what level of claim by itself?
choices: A result independent of its users and setting
A contextual finding with transfer limits
A general design rule established by one case
quiz.answer: A contextual finding with transfer limits
quiz.explain: Local evidence can be valuable without establishing general validity across settings.

quiz.prompt: Which portfolio item demonstrates participation changed the design?
choices: A decision revised through participant evidence
A photograph recording workshop attendance
An invitation list demonstrating outreach intentions
quiz.answer: A decision revised through participant evidence
quiz.explain: A traceable change shows consequential influence more clearly than attendance evidence alone.

quiz.prompt: A civic-space workshop includes regular users, reaches no excluded residents, and has no influence on a fixed proposal. Critique the participation claim and propose a meaningful revision.
quiz.answer: The process provides limited consultation rather than consequential participation. Examine power and recruitment, include excluded residents through accessible formats, and reopen criteria or alternatives they can influence. Document a design decision revised by participant evidence and preserve dissent in the final account.
quiz.explain: The process provides limited consultation rather than consequential participation. Examine power and recruitment, include excluded residents through accessible formats, and reopen criteria or alternatives they can influence. Document a design decision revised by participant evidence and preserve dissent in the final account.
